sourceGuidance.title: MAPsy Scoring
sourceGuidance.text:
The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.
The score itself is not displayed in the report: it is converted to a percentile and assigned a severity band, and the report presents those.

For the Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features scale, the items measuring Anxiousness and Withdrawal are reverse scored before summing, so that low anxiousness and low withdrawal contribute to the scale in the direction that defines the disorder.

sourceGuidance.title: MAPsy Percentiles
sourceGuidance.text:
Percentiles are the primary metric for presenting scores because they are comparable across constructs, regardless of the number of items, and are readily communicated to clients and other professionals. Each score is converted to a percentile against the distribution of scores on that construct in a reference sample drawn from Forbes et al.’s (2025) study. Percentiles can be based on the whole reference sample, All (respondents aged 16 years and over), or on one of two subsets of it, Youth (16 to 24 years) and Adult (25 years and over). The Youth or Adult sample is selected by default from the client’s age at administration, calculated from their date of birth, and the Adult sample is used when no date of birth is entered.
The reference sample is best described as a distress-enriched sample: most of its members were receiving mental health treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community. A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community. A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.
The percentile does not itself say whether a level of psychopathology is clinically significant; that judgement is carried by the severity band. The percentile instead shows how far the client’s level of psychopathology is from what is typical of the reference sample.

sourceGuidance.title: Why are the percentiles based on a mental health sample rather than the general community?
sourceGuidance.text:
The reference sample was recruited for research on mental health; most of its members were receiving treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. This composition suits the measure’s purpose. A measure used to decide whether a presentation warrants further assessment needs to discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, and a sample in which high levels of distress are common represents that range more fully than a general community sample, in which most respondents score near the floor and few score in the range where clinical decisions are made.
This means a percentile compares the client with people who may have been experiencing mental health difficulties, rather than with the general population. A percentile around 50 means a typical level of psychopathology for that group, not an average level for the community.
This is why the severity bands, which are fixed to the score and do not change with the reference sample selected, carry the judgement of whether a level of psychopathology is of clinical interest or clinically significant. The percentile shows where the client sits among people who were, for the most part, receiving mental health treatment.

sourceGuidance.title: Why does the Harmful Substance Use spectrum sometimes show no score?
sourceGuidance.text: Because it is scored only for clients who report using a substance in the past year. Part-way through the questionnaire, the client is asked which substances they have used in the past year, from a checklist of seven classes. A client who selects one or more is then asked nine further items about substance use disorder symptoms and use in dangerous situations, and the Harmful Substance Use spectrum is scored from those items. A client who selects “None of the above” is not asked these items, so the spectrum and its clusters are shown in the report without a score, and the three checklist clusters (Alcohol use, Cannabis use, and Illicit and prescription substance use) are marked No.
